conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/name: Russia's war on Ukraine and the "Russian world" doctrine
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/religionRol: Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 and full-scale invasion in 2022 were driven above all by geopolitics, imperial nationalism and the Kremlin's refusal to accept a sovereign, Western-leaning Ukraine; Vladimir Putin's own justifications centred on NATO, security and the claim that Russians and Ukrainians are 'one people'. Religion enters through the 'Russian world' (russkii mir) ideology, which presents Russia, Ukraine and Belarus as a single civilisation born at the baptism of Kyiv in 988, and through Patriarch Kirill of Moscow's open blessing of the war as a metaphysical struggle against Western decadence. Scholars such as Serhii Plokhy treat religion as one strand of a broader nationalist ideology; Orthodox theologians who signed the 2022 Volos Academy declaration condemned the 'Russian world' teaching as a heresy that had helped prepare the war; others (e.g. Marlene Laruelle) stress that the concept is fluid and largely instrumental, used by the state for soft power. The war has also deepened a church conflict between Moscow and Kyiv over Ukrainian Orthodox independence, so religion is both a legitimising ideology and a field of the conflict, but not its primary cause.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/sides/0/nam: Russian Federation and, in 2014–22, the Russian-backed 'Donetsk' and 'Luhansk People's Republics'
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/sides/0/fai: Majority Russian Orthodox (Moscow Patriarchate) by heritage, with Muslims and others; the war is supported by the Moscow Patriarchate's leadership
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/sides/1/fai: Religiously plural: Orthodox Church of Ukraine, Ukrainian Orthodox Church, Ukrainian Greek Catholics, Roman Catholics, Protestants, Jews and Muslims
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/summary: Russia seized Crimea and fomented war in eastern Ukraine in 2014, then launched a full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022, the largest war in Europe since 1945. The Kremlin's case drew on the 'Russian world' idea of a single Orthodox East Slavic civilisation, and Patriarch Kirill of Moscow framed the war as a holy struggle against Western moral decay, while Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant leaders around the world, and many Orthodox Christians in Ukraine and Russia, condemned it. The war has killed many tens of thousands, devastated Ukrainian cities and deepened the split within world Orthodoxy.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/story:
Both Russia and Ukraine trace their Christianity to the baptism of Prince Volodymyr (Vladimir) of Kyiv in 988. After the Mongol conquest the centre of Rus' Orthodoxy shifted to Moscow; the Metropolis of Kyiv was transferred from the jurisdiction of Constantinople to that of Moscow in 1686, a transfer Constantinople later declared to have been temporary. Under the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union, Ukrainian identity and Ukrainian-language church life were suppressed, and in 1946 the Soviet state forcibly merged the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church into the Russian Orthodox Church. After Ukrainian independence in 1991 Orthodoxy split between the Ukrainian Orthodox Church under Moscow, the Kyiv Patriarchate led from 1995 by Filaret Denysenko, and the small Autocephalous Orthodox Church, while the Greek Catholics re-emerged from the underground.

From the 2000s Russian officials and church leaders promoted the idea of a 'Russian world' (russkii mir): a transnational civilisation of Russian language, culture and Orthodox faith centred on Moscow and including Ukraine and Belarus. Putin created the Russkiy Mir Foundation in 2007, and Patriarch Kirill, elected in 2009, made the concept central to his speeches, describing Kyiv as the 'Jerusalem' of Holy Rus'. When the Euromaidan protests of 2013–14 toppled President Viktor Yanukovych, Ukrainian Greek Catholic and Kyiv Patriarchate clergy prayed on the Maidan and St Michael's Golden-Domed Monastery sheltered protesters. Russia then annexed Crimea in March 2014 and backed armed separatists in Donetsk and Luhansk; in eight years of war in the Donbas over 14,000 people were killed, around 3,400 of them civilians, including the 298 people aboard flight MH17. In occupied areas, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Kyiv Patriarchate, Protestant and Jehovah's Witness communities faced harassment and seizures.

The church conflict escalated in parallel. In 2018 the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople moved to grant independence (autocephaly) to a united Ukrainian church; Moscow broke communion with Constantinople in October 2018, and in January 2019 Patriarch Bartholomew handed the tomos of autocephaly to Metropolitan Epiphanius of the new Orthodox Church of Ukraine. In July 2021 Putin published an essay, 'On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians', which invoked the 'common baptismal font' of 988 and denied that Ukraine had a separate national history.

On 24 February 2022 Russia invaded from the north, east and south. Its attempt to take Kyiv failed and its forces withdrew from the north in late March, leaving behind evidence of mass killings of civilians at Bucha and elsewhere. The siege of Mariupol devastated the city; the drama theatre where hundreds of civilians sheltered was bombed on 16 March. Ukrainian counter-offensives retook Kharkiv province and Kherson in autumn 2022, but the front then largely stabilised in the east and south, with grinding battles at Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Pokrovsk. Russia's missile and drone campaign against cities and power infrastructure has killed thousands of civilians; Russia annexed four Ukrainian provinces in September 2022, and the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023 over the deportation of Ukrainian children. UN monitors also documented abuses by Ukrainian forces, including the ill-treatment and some summary executions of Russian prisoners of war, and civilian deaths from Ukrainian shelling in Russian-held areas, on a much smaller scale.

Patriarch Kirill gave the invasion his public support. In a sermon on 6 March 2022 he described the conflict in Donbas as a 'metaphysical' struggle over whether people would accept Western values such as gay pride parades; in September 2022 he told soldiers that sacrifice in the performance of military duty 'washes away all sins'; and in March 2024 the World Russian People's Council, which he chairs, described the war as a 'holy war' defending Holy Rus' and the world against globalism and 'satanism'. By contrast Metropolitan Onufriy of the Moscow-linked Ukrainian Orthodox Church condemned the invasion on its first day as a repetition of 'the sin of Cain', and in May 2022 his church's council declared its 'full independence' from Moscow while stopping short of autocephaly. Ukraine's government, suspecting some UOC clergy of collaboration, searched its monasteries, prosecuted dozens of clergy and in August 2024 passed a law allowing the banning of religious organisations linked to the Russian Orthodox Church; UN human rights monitors and some religious freedom advocates voiced concern, while Ukrainian authorities called it a matter of national security. In occupied territories Russian authorities closed or seized Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Orthodox Church of Ukraine and Protestant congregations and detained clergy, some of whom were tortured or killed.

The war's human cost has been immense. UN monitors had verified more than 13,000 civilian deaths by mid-2025 and say the true figure is considerably higher; military deaths on both sides number in the hundreds of thousands according to Western estimates. Millions of Ukrainians became refugees or internally displaced, and hundreds of churches, mosques and synagogues were damaged or destroyed. Diplomacy in 2025, including direct Russian–Ukrainian talks in Istanbul and US-brokered efforts, produced large prisoner exchanges but no settlement, and Pope Leo XIV, like Pope Francis before him, repeatedly offered the Holy See's mediation.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/nameOfGod: Russian state and church rhetoric presented the war as the defence of Holy Rus' and traditional Christian values against a decadent, 'satanic' West. Putin invoked the baptism of Kyiv in 988 and in his annexation speech of September 2022 denounced Western 'satanism'; Patriarch Kirill preached that the Donbas conflict was a metaphysical struggle, promised that soldiers who died in their duty would have their sins washed away, and introduced a prayer for the victory of 'Holy Rus'' that clergy were required to read. The Main Cathedral of the Russian Armed Forces at Kubinka, consecrated in 2020, embodied the fusion of military and Orthodox symbolism. On the Ukrainian side clergy of most churches serve as chaplains and the war is widely described as a just war of national defence; the government's measures against the Moscow-linked church were justified as security rather than doctrine.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/religiousCa: The 'Russian world' ideology, embraced by Patriarch Kirill, treats Ukraine as part of a single Orthodox civilisation centred on Moscow and denies its distinct religious and national identity.
The creation of the autocephalous Orthodox Church of Ukraine in 2018–19 was seen in Moscow as a geopolitical defeat and a loss of millions of faithful and historic sites such as Kyiv.
A 'traditional values' discourse shared by the Kremlin and the Moscow Patriarchate framed the West, and a Westward-turning Ukraine, as a moral and spiritual threat.
The close alliance between the Russian state and the Moscow Patriarchate gave the war religious legitimacy and silenced dissenting clergy within Russia.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/otherCauses: Putin's imperial nationalism and his view that the collapse of the Soviet Union was a catastrophe and that Ukraine is not a real nation.
Opposition to NATO enlargement and to Ukraine's movement towards the European Union after 2014.
Fear in the Kremlin that a democratic Ukraine could inspire political change in Russia.
Control of Crimea, the Black Sea Fleet at Sevastopol, the industrial Donbas and land access to Crimea.
Miscalculation of Ukrainian resistance and Western unity based on flawed intelligence.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/triggers/0: The Euromaidan revolution and the flight of President Yanukovych in February 2014, followed by the seizure of Crimea.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/triggers/1: The failure of the Minsk agreements of 2014–15 to settle the Donbas war.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/triggers/2: Russia's military build-up in 2021 and the rejection of its demands for guarantees against NATO enlargement, culminating in recognition of the separatist 'republics' on 21 February 2022.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/0/: Baptism of Prince Volodymyr and the people of Kyiv, the shared origin claimed by both Russian and Ukrainian Orthodoxy.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/1/: The Metropolis of Kyiv is transferred from Constantinople's jurisdiction to Moscow's.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/2/: Putin creates the Russkiy Mir Foundation to promote the 'Russian world'.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/3/: Kirill becomes Patriarch of Moscow and makes the 'Russian world' a central theme.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/4/: Euromaidan; Russia annexes Crimea and war begins in the Donbas.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/5/: Constantinople moves towards Ukrainian autocephaly; Moscow breaks communion with the Ecumenical Patriarchate.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/6/: The Orthodox Church of Ukraine receives its tomos of autocephaly from Patriarch Bartholomew.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/7/: Putin publishes 'On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians'.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/8/: 24 February: full-scale invasion; Metropolitan Onufriy condemns it as 'the sin of Cain'; Kirill's 6 March sermon frames the war as a metaphysical struggle.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/9/: 13 March: Orthodox theologians publish the Volos Academy 'Declaration on the Russian World Teaching'; in May the Ukrainian Orthodox Church declares its independence from Moscow.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/10: Bodies of murdered civilians found in Bucha after Russian withdrawal; Ukraine liberates Kherson in November.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/11: The ICC issues an arrest warrant for Putin over deported children; Ukrainian authorities end the Ukrainian Orthodox Church's lease of the Kyiv Caves Lavra.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/12: The World Russian People's Council calls the war a 'holy war'; Ukraine passes a law enabling bans on Russian Orthodox-affiliated bodies.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/timeline/13: Direct talks in Istanbul bring prisoner exchanges but no peace; Pope Leo XIV offers Vatican mediation.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/keyPeople/0: Ordered the annexation of Crimea and the 2022 invasion, justifying them with history, security claims and the shared baptism of Rus'.
Subject of an ICC arrest warrant since March 2023.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/keyPeople/1: Patriarch of Moscow and All Rus' from 2009
Promoted the 'Russian world' ideology and publicly blessed the war as a struggle against Western values.
Sanctioned by the United Kingdom and several other states; criticised by the Ecumenical Patriarchate, Pope Francis and many member churches of the World Council of Churches.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/keyPeople/2: Led Ukraine's resistance; Russian claims to be 'denazifying' Ukraine ignored his Jewish heritage.
Became a symbol of Ukrainian national defence.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/keyPeople/3: Metropolitan of Kyiv, head of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church (Moscow-linked)
Condemned the invasion on its first day and led his church's May 2022 declaration of independence from Moscow.
His church remains under heavy pressure from the Ukrainian state, while Moscow still counts it as part of the Russian Orthodox Church.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/keyPeople/4: Metropolitan of Kyiv and primate of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine
Head of the autocephalous church since 2018, which supports Ukraine's defence and has received many parishes leaving the Moscow-linked church.
His church is recognised by Constantinople and several other Orthodox churches but not by Moscow.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/keyPeople/5: Major Archbishop of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church
Remained in Kyiv during the invasion, issuing daily video addresses and documenting the war's cost.
A leading voice for Ukraine within the Catholic Church.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/keyPeople/6: Granted autocephaly to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine in 2019 and condemned the invasion and the 'Russian world' ideology.
Remains out of communion with the Moscow Patriarchate.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/keyPeople/7: Refused to read Kirill's prayer for victory and spoke for peace.
Removed from his parish and defrocked by a church court in January 2024.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/casualties/: No reliable overall figure exists while the war continues. For 2014–21 the UN human rights office (OHCHR) counted about 14,000 conflict-related deaths, about 3,400 of them civilians. Since February 2022 the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission had verified more than 13,000 civilian deaths by mid-2025, stating that the real number is higher, especially in occupied Mariupol. Military deaths are state secrets; the independent outlet Mediazona and BBC Russian had confirmed by name more than 100,000 Russian soldiers killed by mid-2025, and Western government and think-tank estimates (e.g. CSIS, 2025) put Russian military deaths at several hundred thousand and Ukrainian military deaths at tens of thousands to around 100,000. These figures are contested and should be treated as rough.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/effects/0: Millions of Ukrainians fled abroad or were internally displaced, and large areas of eastern and southern Ukraine were devastated or occupied.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/effects/1: Russia became subject to extensive Western sanctions and deepened its alignment with China, Iran and North Korea.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/effects/2: Finland and Sweden joined NATO, and European states greatly increased defence spending.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/effects/3: The International Criminal Court and national courts opened investigations into war crimes, including the deportation of Ukrainian children.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/effects/4: Ukrainian national identity, including use of the Ukrainian language and church independence, was greatly strengthened.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/effectsOnCh: Hundreds of churches and other religious sites were damaged or destroyed, according to Ukrainian and international monitors.
Large numbers of parishes moved from the Moscow-linked Ukrainian Orthodox Church to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine, and the UOC distanced itself from Moscow.
The schism between Moscow and Constantinople deepened, and Orthodox churches worldwide were forced to take positions on Kirill's support for the war.
The 'Russian world' teaching was condemned by many Orthodox theologians as ethno-phyletism, a heresy condemned by Constantinople in 1872.
Russian clergy who opposed the war were fined, suspended or defrocked, while some emigrated or joined other jurisdictions.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/legacy: The war is the clearest twenty-first-century case of a Christian church leadership blessing a war of aggression against a largely Christian neighbour, and it has provoked intense debate within Orthodoxy about nationalism, church–state 'symphony' and the theology of the nation. It has also brought renewed reflection on just war and on the duties of churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, to resist the sacralising of violence.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/dissenters/: Hundreds of Orthodox theologians worldwide condemned the 'Russian world' teaching in March 2022 as a heresy that sanctifies ethnic and national power.
Head of the Moscow-linked church in Ukraine who called the invasion fratricide and 'the sin of Cain' and appealed to Putin to stop the war.
Nearly 300 Russian Orthodox priests and deacons signed a public appeal in March 2022 calling for reconciliation and an end to the war.
Village priest in the Kostroma region fined in 2022 for an anti-war sermon and online statement and subsequently removed from his parish.
Moscow priest who refused to read the prayer for victory and was defrocked in 2024.
Repeatedly condemned the war, warned Kirill not to become 'Putin's altar boy' and sent envoys on humanitarian missions.

conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/theatres/2/: Kyiv: St Michael's Golden-Domed Monastery and the Caves Lavra

conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/campaigns/0: The Russian assault on Kyiv, February–March 2022

Russian airborne and armoured forces attacked towards Kyiv through the Chornobyl zone and Hostomel but were halted at Irpin; when they withdrew at the end of March, hundreds of murdered civilians were found in Bucha and neighbouring towns.
conflicts/russia-ukraine-war/campaigns/1: Forces from Crimea captured Kherson and Melitopol in the first days and besieged Mariupol, which fell in May 2022 after the defenders of the Azovstal steelworks surrendered; Kherson city was retaken by Ukraine in November.
